## TL;DR

The pressure panel showed ratios for every state, but normal had no explanation and warning did not tell users whether it held work. The Control dashboard now describes all three states in plain language, and `repoos stats` reports the same distinction. I added stable normal, warning, and critical preview fixtures and verified each at desktop and mobile widths using headless Chromium against the auth-less scratch server. The final responsive sweep passed at 1280px and 375px with no horizontal overflow or browser errors.

## Work and rationale

I started with the guard's documented contract and current panel behavior. The distinction matters: warning readings are advisory, and high swap/compressor occupancy by itself does not block starts. Critical means a blocking signal is active and new work waits; it does not mean existing agents are stopped. I used that contract to guide both the wording and synthetic fixtures rather than implying that any elevated percentage automatically stops work.

The panel previously rendered its alert only for warning and critical. Normal readings appeared in the Machine line as “Pressure: normal” plus three ratios, which named a state but did not explain what it meant. I made the pressure summary visible for every state. Normal now says there is no pressure hold and that the memory figures are context. Warning says work can continue and that the warning is advisory. Critical says new work is held until the blocking signals ease, while running agents continue. Existing reason/warning text stays visible because it tells the operator which signal produced the state. The banner keeps the same ratios in each state, so a normal baseline can be compared directly with a warning or hold.

The `repoos stats` command already printed level, ratios, source, and a guard reason. It did not explain the operational effect for normal or warning, and critical’s reason alone could require interpretation. I added one concise explanation per level after the pressure row: clear, advisory only, or holding. Existing reason output and the heavy-job count remain alongside it. This keeps the dashboard and CLI consistent while retaining the detailed signal needed to diagnose the machine.

For repeatable UI review, I registered three preview-only system fixtures. They share the same 16 GB machine baseline and vary available memory, load, swap, compressor, paging, and heavy-job counts by state. Warning emphasizes high swap and compressor occupancy with no paging hold. Critical supplies low availability and active paging, while normal remains quiet. The fixture values are synthetic and are not presented as live machine measurements. Component tests cover their displayed meanings and key readings; CLI tests cover the three state explanations.

I wrote the observed scenarios and limits to `docs/qa/2026-11-pressure-states.md`. The doc records the viewport sizes, fixture states, rendered status, no-overflow result, and the difference between an initial mobile viewport and the scrolled panel view. It explicitly limits its claim to a synthetic UI pass rather than a real stress test.

## Approaches tried

I first used the existing component and CLI tests to map current output and verify how the panel formats percentages. I then added fixtures and table-driven assertions before starting a browser server. An initial test expectation used decimal percentage precision, but the panel intentionally rounds ratios to whole percentages. I adjusted the assertions to match visible output, keeping the test focused on the user-facing text rather than an internal float representation.

I ran `just serve-noauth 7273` from a temporary scratch worktree with the patch applied. In headless Playwright Chromium, I visited the Control dashboard for normal, warning, and critical at 1280×900 and 375×900. Each route returned HTTP 200, exposed the expected state banner, and had no page or panel horizontal overflow. I also captured the mobile warning after scrolling it into view. The initial top-of-page capture showed the lower half of that banner beneath the fixed bottom navigation because the dashboard was still at the top. Scrolling the panel into view showed the whole explanation above the navigation; this is normal vertical page scrolling, not clipped text.

## Challenges and blockers

The scratch worktree had no installed dependencies, so its first serve attempt could not compile the newly added test. Installing the locked dependencies in the scratch worktree resolved that environment issue. Its subsequent typecheck caught a missing explicit `reason: null` in the partial pressure view used by a CLI test; I added the required field and reran the preview build successfully.

The first component run also caught two mistaken ratio expectations: 12.5% and 43.75% render as 13% and 44%. These were test expectation errors, not display defects. I updated the expected text to the actual precision and reran the focused suites successfully. The first remote scoped gate then found one assertion typo: the fixture wording says occupancy “does not” hold work, while the test expected “do not.” I corrected the assertion to match the displayed sentence and confirmed the focused suites passed again.

The first complete check also caught a hard-coded-color rule violation in the normal banner tint: its fallback literal produces an unsuitable near-white background in light themes. I removed the tint and kept the state banner on the neutral panel surface. The complete scoped check then passed, including remote tests, rendered contrast, and UI smoke. No human or live-host step was required.

## Key learnings

Pressure labels should state their effect on work, especially because a warning does not block starts while a critical verdict does. Occupancy percentages are useful context but can mislead without that distinction. Normal deserves an explicit interpretation too; otherwise, users see metrics without knowing whether RepoOS is holding work.

Deterministic preview fixtures make pressure states comparable without changing the machine’s actual load. The fixtures also expose the mobile reading order: Machine details and the alert are below earlier dashboard sections, so responsive QA should inspect the alert after scrolling it into view as well as checking for horizontal overflow. The current panel remains readable at 375px once brought into view.

The focused component and resource reporting test run passed 14 tests. The auth-less preview build and six desktop/mobile Playwright visits also passed without browser errors or horizontal overflow. A real-device interaction pass or live system stress test was not performed and is not claimed by this report.
